To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
σG can become active without σF and SpoIIGA and that its activity is confined largely to the mother cell when it becomes active without σF.
σG can become active in the mother cells in the absence of the anti-sigma factors SpoIIAB or SpoIIIGA and that pro-σE can counteract the inhibitory effects of SpoIIIGA on σG activation.
in spoIIAB deletion strains lacking both σF in the mother cell and pro-σF in the presporangium, σE is not activated, but σG is, and its activity is largely in the mother cell.
In summary, our research is concerned with
control of the expression and location of σG and its role in the control of the mother cell program.
control of the location of the sporulation-specific σ factor σG.
the mechanisms by which σG is prevented from being active in the mother cells during the engulfment phase, and how σE and SpoIIGA are involved in this process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
σF and SpoIIGA are required for σG to become active only in the prespores and not in mother cells.

the control of σG expression and activity during sporulation is a complex process that depends upon the activities of σF in conjunction with SpoIIGA to promote the appearance of σE in the prespores, the activity of σE in conjunction with SpoIIAA and SpoIIAB in the mother cell to promote the appearance and activation of σF in prespores, and the activity of σF to promote the appearance, activation, and localization of σG to the prespores.
the activity of σG in the mother cell is prevented by SpoIIGA and that this is counteracted by σE.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the activity of σG during sporulation is controlled by a complex network of factors that include σF, σE, SpoIIAB, and SpoIIGA and that these factors are not all needed for σG activation but are required for σG activation in the prespores.
σG becomes active only when it is needed, and it is controlled in a way that it is active only in the prespores when needed, and only in the mother cells when needed.

σG becomes active in the prespores in wild-type strains and in the mother cells in spoIIA strains, and this switch in compartmentalization is controlled by the activity of SpoIIG and SpoIIAB, respectively, in the mother cell and by the presence of σE.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the compartmentalization of σF and of σE in the prespores and mother cells, respectively, is not the only determinant of the location of σE and σG activity in sporulation.
σG activity is controlled in two ways, one in which σE activity in the mother cell is necessary for σG activation and the other in which σG activity is prevented by SpoIIIGA.
the compartmentalization and timing of σG activity is controlled by the activities of regulators of σF and of σE, and by the location of the σG structural gene.
